section_summary: This section comprises State Department correspondence, diplomatic despatches, legal memoranda, and cross-reference sheets concerning Japanese income taxation affecting American interests between 1931 and 1937. Key matters examined include the method of assessing excess income tax on American insurance companies and branch offices under Japanese law and the 1911 commercial treaty, taxation of perpetual lease properties in Yokohama, and income tax liability of U.S. government personnel and Christian missionaries. Diplomatic and consular officers repeatedly assessed whether Japanese tax laws were discriminatory or in violation of treaty rights, generally concluding that formal international protests were unwarranted because American firms suffered little practical harm and could claim U.S. foreign tax credits.

subfiles.about: Recommends filing the Tokyo Embassy's despatch on Japanese excess income tax without action pending a direct request from affected insurance companies.
subfiles.from: Office of the Solicitor, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Recommends filing the despatch without action because the issue is academic and insurance companies have not directly requested relief.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Assessment of Excess Income Tax on American Insurance Companies in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports on unofficial negotiations regarding the Japanese method of assessing excess income tax on American insurance companies operating in Japan.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Reports on Japanese methods of assessing excess income tax on American insurance companies depositing exempt bonds. Recommends against further diplomatic intervention since no discrimination exists and companies should pursue standard claims channels.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 203: Method Employed by Japanese Tax Authorities to Assess Excess Income Tax on American Insurance Companies

subfiles.about: Summarizes a conference with Japanese Finance Department officials regarding the computation of excess income tax and treatment of deposited bonds.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Dooman summarizes his conference with Finance Ministry tax official Hoshino concerning formulae for calculating branch capital and deposited bond interest. Japanese officials maintained their statutory interpretation treated all companies with non-taxable income equally, leaving no basis for formal diplomatic protest without Department authorization.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 203: Letter from Eugene H. Dooman to W. W. Glass Regarding Conference with Japanese Tax Officials
subfiles.to: W. W. Glass, Acting Manager for Japan, The Home Insurance Company

subfiles.about: Notes agreement of FE and Le with Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 298 and Consulate General Despatch No. 236.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Notes that Far Eastern Affairs and the Legal Adviser agree with the Tokyo Embassy and Consulate General despatches.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatches Concerning Japanese Income Tax on Foreign Juridical Persons
subfiles.to: Office of the Legal Adviser and Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Discusses Consul Dickover's report alleging treaty discrimination in Japanese corporation taxes and recommends against making it an international issue.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Transmits Commercial Attaché Butts's analysis of Consul Dickover's report on Japanese income taxes. Neville concludes legal discrimination would be difficult to establish, American firms suffer no practical injury, and the issue does not warrant international dispute.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 298: Income Taxes Levied on American Juridical Persons Doing Business in Japan

subfiles.about: Analyzes the comparative tax burden of domestic Japanese corporations versus American branch offices through theoretical ten-year balance sheets.
subfiles.from: Halleck A. Butts, Commercial Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Butts evaluates Consul Dickover's report and presents theoretical calculations comparing a Japanese subsidiary with an American branch office. He concludes that net financial returns vary negligibly between organizational forms and that the Japanese tax law results in substantially equal tax revenues to both governments.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 298: Letter from Commercial Attaché Halleck A. Butts to Edwin L. Neville on Japanese Income Tax Law
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: True copy of Despatch No. 298 discussing Japanese taxation of American corporations and recommending against raising an international issue.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: True copy of Embassy Despatch No. 298 reviewing Consul Dickover's views on Japanese corporate income tax and advising against diplomatic protest.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 298 (Copy): Income Taxes Levied on American Juridical Persons Doing Business in Japan

subfiles.about: Copy of Commercial Attaché Butts's letter analyzing the comparative economic effects of Japanese corporate taxation on branches versus subsidiaries.
subfiles.from: Halleck A. Butts, Commercial Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Duplicate copy of Commercial Attaché Butts's detailed letter analyzing Japanese corporate taxation through ten-year theoretical models. The calculations show minimal aggregate differences between domestic subsidiaries and foreign branches, demonstrating that tax considerations rarely dictate corporate form.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 298 (Copy): Letter from Commercial Attaché Halleck A. Butts to Edwin L. Neville
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Counselor of Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Concurs that alleged tax discrimination cannot be established as a matter of law and suggests consulting the Treasury Department.
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Agrees that legal discrimination is difficult to prove and suggests consulting the Treasury regarding potential U.S. tax amendments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Alleged Discrimination in Japan in Favor of Japanese Corporations in Matters of Taxation
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Reports that Japan's higher basic income tax rate on foreign corporate branches may violate the 1911 treaty and proposes reciprocal U.S. tax legislation.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Dickover reports that the Japanese Income Tax Law assesses a 10% basic tax on foreign branches compared to 5% on domestic juridical persons, arguing this may violate Article I of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation. He notes American corporations do not complain because foreign tax payments are credited against U.S. taxes, shifting the financial burden to the U.S. Treasury. To achieve reciprocity, he proposes amending U.S. tax law to levy an equivalent retaliatory tax on American branches of Japanese corporations.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1042: Apparent Violation of Treaty Rights in the Japanese Income Tax Law

subfiles.about: Reviews the Tokyo round-table conference on Japanese corporate income tax and recommends referring the correspondence to EA and Le.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Reviews findings of the Tokyo conference on Consul Dickover's despatch, agreeing that making an international issue is unwarranted, and forwards correspondence to the Economic Adviser and Legal Adviser.
subfiles.title: Memorandum Regarding Apparent Violation of Treaty Rights in the Japan Income Tax Law
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Transmits Consul Dickover's despatch and advises a policy of non-interference regarding Japanese corporate income taxes.
subfiles.from: Arthur Garrels, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Garrels concurs that technically a treaty violation exists but advises a policy of 'quieta non movere' because American interests suffer no injury and Treasury losses are insignificant.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 236: Apparent Violation of Treaty Rights in the Japanese Income Tax Law

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 92 regarding Japanese income tax on American officials and the case of Truman M. Martin.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 92 concerning Japanese income tax on American officials, specifically Truman M. Martin.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 92 Regarding Japanese Income Tax on American Government Officials

subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese tax authorities demanding income tax from non-diplomatic U.S. personnel and suggests reciprocal taxation on Japanese officials in America.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that Japan assesses income tax on non-diplomatic American personnel, including Quartermaster Clerk Truman M. Martin. He transmits a list of unattached Japanese government offices in the United States for potential reciprocal taxation.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 92: Japanese Income Tax Imposed on American Government Officials

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 274 regarding perpetual lease property taxation and letter to Dr. Whiting S. Worden.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 274 regarding taxation of rental income from perpetual lease property held by Dr. Worden.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 274 Regarding Taxation on Incomes Derived from Perpetual Lease Property in Japan

subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of the Embassy's letter to Dr. Whiting S. Worden regarding Japanese income tax on perpetual lease rentals.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Transmits Embassy letter to Dr. Whiting S. Worden concerning his liability for Japanese income taxes on perpetual lease rentals.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 274: Taxation on Incomes Derived from Perpetual Lease Property in Japan

subfiles.about: Explains the legal status of perpetual lease properties and clarifies that income taxes on rental income are not exempt under treaties or the Hague Award.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that perpetual leases and the Hague Award exempt land and buildings from direct property taxes but not personal income derived from rental proceeds. He clarifies that no treaty right is violated and declines diplomatic protest unless Worden proves nationality-based discrimination.
subfiles.title: Enclosure to Despatch No. 274: Letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew to Dr. Whiting S. Worden

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 689 regarding Japanese income tax laws.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet for Tokyo Despatch No. 689 transmitting information on Japanese income tax laws.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 689 Regarding Income Tax Laws of Japan

subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese Foreign Office note on reciprocal tax provisions under the U.S. Revenue Act of 1932.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits a Foreign Office note regarding reciprocal tax provisions under the Revenue Act of 1932 and offers to procure de Becker's English translation of Japanese income tax laws.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 689: Income Tax Laws

subfiles.about: Explains Japanese law on foreign tax credits and exemptions for American shipping earnings under the reciprocal arrangement of 1926.
subfiles.from: Koki Hirota, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.summary: Foreign Minister Hirota clarifies that Japanese law grants no foreign tax credit to resident Americans, but exempts earnings from American-registered ships under the 1926 reciprocal agreement.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1 to Despatch No. 689: Note No. 13/T2 from Foreign Minister Koki Hirota to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for Despatch No. 113 regarding non-diplomatic employee tax lists furnished to Kobe tax authorities.
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Kobe (Scott)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet regarding employee tax data provided to Kobe authorities while British, German, and French consulates ignored requests.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 113 Regarding Employee Information Furnished Japanese Tax Authorities

subfiles.about: Inquires about the legality of Japan taxing salaries of American Presbyterian missionaries funded from the United States.
subfiles.from: C. Darby Fulton, Executive Secretary, Presbyterian Committee of Foreign Missions
subfiles.summary: Fulton inquires about the legality of Japanese taxation of American missionary salaries and whether similar rules apply in the Belgian Congo, China, Brazil, and Mexico.
subfiles.title: Letter from C. Darby Fulton to Secretary of State Cordell Hull Regarding Taxation of Missionaries in Japan

subfiles.about: Explains international tax principles, 1911 treaty protections, China extraterritorial exemptions, and U.S. foreign tax credit provisions.
subfiles.from: Department of State (For the Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State explains that nations generally have the right to tax resident aliens absent treaty exemptions. It cites non-discrimination under the 1911 Japanese treaty, notes China's income tax does not apply to Americans, and quotes Section 131 of the Revenue Act of 1936 regarding foreign tax credits.
subfiles.title: Letter from Department of State to C. Darby Fulton Regarding Income Taxation of American Missionaries Abroad
subfiles.to: C. Darby Fulton, Executive Secretary, Presbyterian Committee of Foreign Missions
